subject: chemistry
title: Aldehydes and ketones
key_idea: Aldehydes and ketones contain a polar C=O group. Aldehydes are easily oxidised, ketones are not, and both are reduced to alcohols. Their carbon atom is attacked by nucleophiles such as H⁻ and CN⁻, which is nucleophilic addition.

sections.heading: The carbonyl group and physical properties

blocks.text: Both families contain the carbonyl group, C=O. This section covers how to tell them apart and how the group affects boiling point and solubility.

items.meaning: The C=O group is at the end of the chain, so the carbon has one H attached: R–CHO.
The C=O group is inside the chain, joined to two carbon atoms: R–CO–R'.

items: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so C=O is **polar**: Cδ+ and Oδ−.
Aldehydes and ketones have no O–H or N–H bond, so they do **not** form hydrogen bonds with each other.
Their molecules attract each other by permanent dipole–dipole forces and London forces.
Boiling points are higher than alkanes of similar size, but lower than alcohols, which do hydrogen bond.
The lone pair on the oxygen can form a hydrogen bond with a δ+ hydrogen in water.
Short-chain aldehydes and ketones are therefore **soluble** in water.
Solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain gets longer.
Aldehyde: R–CHO at the end of the chain. Ketone: R–CO–R' inside the chain.
No intermolecular hydrogen bonds, so boiling points are lower than alcohols.
They hydrogen bond with water, so small ones dissolve.

blocks.text: Alcohols are oxidised to carbonyl compounds. Only aldehydes can be oxidised further. In equations the oxidising agent is written as [O].

rows: Acidified dichromate(VI), heat and distil off the aldehyde as it forms

blocks.label: Oxidation of an aldehyde
where: [O] = oxygen supplied by the oxidising agent

items: Distilling the aldehyde out as it forms stops it being oxidised to the acid.
Refluxing with excess oxidant gives the carboxylic acid.
A ketone has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, so it resists oxidation.
Acidified dichromate(VI) turns from **orange** to **green** (Cr³⁺) when it oxidises something.
Primary alcohol gives an aldehyde, then a carboxylic acid.
Secondary alcohol gives a ketone, which is not oxidised further.
Distil to stop at the aldehyde, reflux to reach the acid.

blocks.text: Carbonyl compounds are reduced to alcohols and react with cyanide. Both are nucleophilic addition, because the nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon.

items: Reducing agents: NaBH₄ in aqueous solution, or LiAlH₄ in dry ether.
Aldehydes are reduced to **primary** alcohols.
Ketones are reduced to **secondary** alcohols.
In equations the reducing agent is written as [H].

items.text: A hydride ion, H⁻, from the reducing agent uses its lone pair to attack the δ+ carbon.
The C=O π bond breaks. Both electrons move onto oxygen, giving a negative intermediate.
The O⁻ takes a hydrogen ion from water (or dilute acid) to form the alcohol.

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN, with KCN as a catalyst, to form hydroxynitriles. The attacking nucleophile is the cyanide ion, CN⁻.

items.text: CN⁻ uses its lone pair on carbon to attack the δ+ carbon of C=O.
The C=O π bond breaks and its electrons move onto oxygen, giving an O⁻ intermediate.
The O⁻ takes H⁺ from water or HCN, forming the hydroxynitrile and regenerating CN⁻.

items: The C=O group is planar, so CN⁻ can attack from either side with equal chance.
Aldehydes and **unsymmetrical** ketones give a new chiral carbon, so two enantiomers form in equal amounts.
This racemic mixture does not rotate plane-polarised light, so it has no optical activity.
A symmetrical ketone such as propanone gives a product with no chiral carbon.
Aldehyde gives a primary alcohol, ketone a secondary alcohol.
Both reductions and the HCN reaction are nucleophilic addition.
Attack from either side of the planar C=O gives a racemic mixture.

blocks.text: Four tests identify carbonyl compounds. Pick a compound to see what each test gives.

diagram.alt: A predictor. Pick a carbonyl compound to see the result of Tollens' reagent, Fehling's solution, 2,4-DNPH and alkaline iodine.

options.label: Ethanal, CH₃CHO
options.explanation: An aldehyde, so it is oxidised by Tollens' and Fehling's. It contains CH₃CO, so it gives the iodine test.

options.label: Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO
options.explanation: An aldehyde, so it is oxidised. It has no CH₃CO group, so the iodine test is negative.

options.label: Propanone, CH₃COCH₃
options.explanation: A ketone, so it is not oxidised. It contains CH₃CO, so it gives the iodine test.

options.label: Pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃
options.explanation: A ketone, so it is not oxidised. It has no CH₃CO group, so the iodine test is negative.

items: Tollens' reagent: the aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylic acid and Ag⁺ is reduced to silver: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag.
Fehling's or Benedict's: the aldehyde is oxidised and blue Cu²⁺ is reduced to red Cu₂O.
Ketones give no change with Tollens' or Fehling's, because they are not easily oxidised.
2,4-DNPH gives a precipitate with aldehydes and ketones, so it does not tell them apart.

items.text: Add 2,4-DNPH. An orange or yellow solid shows a carbonyl group.
Filter and recrystallise the solid, then dry it.
Measure its melting point and compare it with a data table of derivatives to identify the carbonyl compound.

items: Alkaline iodine is I₂ with NaOH. A yellow precipitate of tri-iodomethane, CHI₃, shows a CH₃CO group in an aldehyde or ketone, CH₃CO–R.
Ethanal is the only aldehyde that gives it. Propanone and butanone are examples of ketones that do.
2,4-DNPH detects C=O. Tollens' and Fehling's separate aldehydes from ketones.
Aldehydes reduce the reagent, so they are oxidised to carboxylic acids.
A yellow precipitate with alkaline iodine shows CH₃CO.

checks.q: Explain why propanone is soluble in water but does not form hydrogen bonds with other propanone molecules.
checks.a: The oxygen lone pair forms hydrogen bonds with the δ+ hydrogen of water, so it dissolves. Propanone has no O–H or N–H bond, so it has no δ+ hydrogen to hydrogen bond with another propanone molecule.

checks.q: Describe a test that distinguishes pentanal from pentan-2-one, and give the observation with each.
checks.a: Warm with Tollens' reagent (or Fehling's solution). Pentanal gives a silver mirror (brick-red precipitate); pentan-2-one gives no change.

checks.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethanal with HCN and KCN, and explain why the product is a racemic mixture.
checks.a: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O with its lone pair. The C=O π bond breaks and the electrons move onto oxygen, giving an O⁻ intermediate, which is protonated by H₂O or HCN to give CH₃CH(OH)CN. C=O is planar, so CN⁻ attacks from either side equally, giving equal amounts of two enantiomers.

blocks.text: This part covers the reagents in the form they are written in equations.

items: Oxidising agent: Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺, which is K₂Cr₂O₇ with H₂SO₄. Write [O] in equations.
NaBH₄ reduces the carbonyl to an alcohol. The nucleophile is the hydride ion, H⁻, and the intermediate is protonated by H₂O.
HCN is made from NaCN(aq)/H⁺(aq). The first attack is by CN⁻, then the intermediate is protonated by H₂O or H⁺.
For Tollens' reagent, [O] is acceptable in equations.

blocks.text: This part covers how to show the HCN mechanism and the reagents for each test.

items: Draw the mechanism with curly arrows, the lone pair on CN⁻ and the dipole on C=O.
Optical activity is the evidence: the product mixture does not rotate plane-polarised light, because the two enantiomers are equal in amount.
Lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) in dry ether reduces the carbonyl. It reacts with water, so the ether must be dry.
Benedict's solution can be used in place of Fehling's solution.

blocks.text: This part covers the hazards of KCN and how to write the overall equations.

items: KCN is **highly toxic**. It releases poisonous HCN gas on contact with acid, so it must be handled in a fume cupboard with gloves.
Write overall reduction equations with [H], as shown above.
Write the HCN equations as carbonyl + HCN → hydroxynitrile.
In the hydride mechanism, show H⁻ as the nucleophile attacking the C=O carbon.
The hydroxynitrile is made with KCN followed by dilute acid. The cyanide ion attacks first, and the dilute acid then supplies the H⁺ that protonates the intermediate.

blocks.text: This part covers the reagents and conditions, and the full iodine test equation.

items: Acidified KMnO₄ can be used instead of acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ to oxidise alcohols. Distil to obtain an aldehyde or a ketone.
NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ reduce aldehydes and ketones to alcohols.
HCN needs a little KCN as catalyst, and heat. The examples are ethanal and propanone.
Ease of oxidation, together with Fehling's and Tollens' reagents, is used to deduce whether an unknown carbonyl compound is an aldehyde or a ketone.
